title: Pain the medicine
hookLine: pain became the medicine and pleasure the disease (Asa di Var, ang 469)

lines: WHEN DID YOU CHANGE THE MOST?
cards: Ask people when they changed the most, and very few will name the year everything went well. They'll name the breakup, the layoff, the hospital waiting room, the year a parent died.
Nobody would choose those seasons, or wish them on anyone. And yet, looking back, many people say: that's when I woke up. That's when I found out who my friends were, or what I believed.
Guru Nanak put that strange experience into one line of the Asa di Var, and it still startles people.

teach.b: The salok is on ang 469. Its opening line, in paraphrase: pain has become the medicine, and pleasure the disease, because where there is pleasure, there is no longing for you. Dukh daaroo, sukh rog.
Dukh is pain, sorrow, suffering. Daaroo is medicine. Sukh is comfort, pleasure, ease.
Rog is disease. This line is easy to misread, so slow down.

Guru Nanak isn't saying pain is good, or that people deserve to suffer, or that anyone should go looking for it. Sikh teaching doesn't praise hurting yourself; the Gurus turned away from harsh self-punishment as a path.

And in Sikh life, relieving other people's pain is a duty: the langar feeds the hungry, and Sikhs have long run free kitchens and clinics in disasters. The line is about what comfort can do to the heart.
When everything is easy, it's easy to forget the One.
Ease can make us sleepy. Pain, the salok says, often does the opposite. It breaks the illusion that we're in control, and turns the heart toward the One.
Then the salok goes on, still in paraphrase: you are the Doer; I am nothing; if I try to do it myself, nothing happens.
And a line that connects back to day five hundred forty-two: I am a sacrifice to you, dwelling in your kudrat, your creation; your limits can't be known.
So the medicine isn't the pain itself. It's what pain can open: the end of pretending we run the world, and a turn toward the One who does.

how: Sikhs hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and many recall dukh daaroo, sukh rog in hard times as a reminder that suffering can turn the heart toward the One.

o: a fast kept for spiritual merit

games.q: inside the line — tap the pairs.

s: the salok teaches that people should seek out pain
it says ease can make us forget the One; it doesn't praise hurting yourself.
the salok says where there is pleasure there is no longing for the One
that's why it calls pleasure the disease.
the salok mentions kudrat, the creation
I am a sacrifice to you, dwelling in your kudrat.

games.q: life has been easy for months, and you've stopped thinking about the One. what does the salok call that ease?
games.why: dukh daaroo, sukh rog: pain became the medicine, pleasure the disease, because in pleasure there's no longing for the One.

practice: Think of a hard season that is now behind you, not the hardest, and not one that still feels raw; if nothing comes, just rest in the breath.
If one does, don't relive it; ask one quiet question, what did that season turn me toward, and let the answer be small. If you pray, say Waheguru, for what you learned and for who helped.

wordCard.voice: Dukh, pain or sorrow: in Guru Nanak's salok, dukh daaroo, sukh rog, pain can turn the heart toward the One, while ease can make it forget.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pain the medicine, pleasure the disease; the opening of the salok.

carryVoice: Your line: you are the Doer. The medicine is what pain can open. Five hundred fifty days, and counting.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (dukh daaroo sukh rog bhaiaa), Ang 469
